name: Simpro
tagline: End-to-end job management for trade and field service businesses: quoting, scheduling, timesheets, inventory, invoicing.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Simpro is sold via quote, typically scaled by user count and modules.

verdictSummary: Simpro is not an app, it is the operating system for an electrical or plumbing or HVAC business with a dozen vans on the road. The surface area is quotes to jobs to schedules to techs' mobile timesheets to stock movements to progress invoices to accounting sync, all of it needing to agree with each other and with the tax authority. An agent can absolutely build you a nice job tracker in a sitting, and if you are a solo operator with a notebook and a ute, that might genuinely be enough. What it cannot build is the offline-capable field app your techs will actually use, the Xero or QuickBooks reconciliation, the supplier catalogue pricing feeds, or the audit trail your accountant and insurer expect. The moment a second person depends on the data, the DIY version becomes the most expensive thing you own.
coreLoopDIY: A local single-user job book: create a customer, quote it, log labour hours and materials against the job, and export an invoice PDF.
requirements: Node 20 and a machine you control
Willingness to do your own backups
Manual re-entry into whatever accounting software you already use
whatYouLose: A field-ready mobile app that works in a basement with no signal and syncs later
Accounting integration, so every invoice becomes double data entry
Supplier price catalogues and live stock levels across vans and warehouse
Multi-user scheduling, dispatch and the audit trail that comes with it
Someone to call when the thing that runs your cashflow stops working
moatNotes: Once your job history, stock and invoicing live in one system, leaving means reconstructing years of records mid-quarter. Nobody does that voluntarily.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the software is not the product, the absence of chaos is. A trades business running twenty jobs a week pays Simpro so that the quote a tech saw on their phone is the same quote that got invoiced, so that hours logged become payroll, so that stock leaving the van shows up somewhere. That chain is boring, tedious and enormous, and every link is a place where a homegrown tool quietly loses money. The cost of the subscription is trivially smaller than one week of unbilled labour.
notes: A solo tradie can replace maybe fifteen percent of this in a weekend and be fine. The moat is the chain from quote to timesheet to stock to invoice to accounting sync, and the fact that a whole crew's day depends on it staying unbroken.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user job book for a solo tradesperson. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/jobs.db, migrations in plain SQL on boot
- Tailwind for styling, no component library
- Runs with `npm run dev` on localhost only

Data model:
- customers: name, phone, email, site address, notes
- jobs: customer_id, title, status (quoted, scheduled, in_progress, invoiced, paid), scheduled_date, description
- labour_entries: job_id, date, hours, hourly_rate, description
- material_entries: job_id, description, qty, unit_cost, markup_pct
- settings: business name, ABN or tax id, default hourly rate, default markup, tax rate, payment terms text

Screens:
1. Today: jobs scheduled for today and the next 7 days, plus anything in_progress
2. Jobs list with status filter and search
3. Job detail: header info, labour table with inline add, materials table with inline add, live totals (labour + materials with markup, tax, grand total), status dropdown
4. Customers list and detail with their job history
5. Settings

Quote and invoice output:
- One route that renders a clean printable HTML document for a job, styled for A4 print, with a Quote mode and an Invoice mode
- Print to PDF via the browser. Do not add a PDF library.

Explicitly out of scope: mobile app, offline sync, multi-user, accounting integrations, supplier catalogues, payments, email sending, recurring maintenance schedules.

Include a `npm run backup` script that copies the SQLite file to ./backups with a timestamp. Put nothing secret in code; if you add anything configurable, use .env.local and ship .env.example. Seed the database with two fake customers and three jobs so the UI is not empty on first run. Write a short README covering how to run it, where the data lives, and the fact that backups are the user's problem.
